title: Data Management in WSN-CPS (Module 6) — Full Exam Revision
description: Exam revision of Module 6 data management in cyber-physical systems with wireless sensor networks: WSN-CPS definition and components, WSN vs WSN-CPS data management, constraints, the comparison table, data collection with mobile elements, controlled and uncontrolled mobility, processing, storage, querying, compression and analysis.

pronounce.WSN-CPS: W S N C P S
pronounce.CPS-WSNs: C P S W S Ns

scenes.title: Module 6 overview
lines: Module six covers data management activities, resource allocation, game theory, and cooperative relaying.
This video is the data management part: data management in cyber physical systems with wireless sensor networks.
We will cover every slide, from the definition of WSN-CPS to data analysis.

scenes.title: What is a WSN-CPS?
lines: First, a cyber physical system, or CPS, is a system that integrates the cyber and physical worlds to interact with the real world.
A WSN-CPS is a cyber physical system that integrates physical and cyber components through wireless sensor networks.
The role of the WSN in a CPS: it ensures communication between the physical and cyber components, for efficient data collection and actuation.
Applications are systems that need monitoring and control, in areas like environmental management.

scenes.title: Four components of WSN-CPS
lines: A WSN-CPS has four components.
The sensing component collects and transmits data from the physical environment.
The cyber component analyzes the data and determines the necessary actions.
The actuation component executes actions in the physical environment, based on the cyber system's instructions.
And the communication component manages data transfer between all the components.
Notice the loop: sense, analyze, act, and communicate in between.

scenes.title: WSN vs WSN-CPS: goal
lines: How does data management differ between a plain WSN and a WSN-CPS?
The goal of a WSN is passive monitoring of the physical environment.
The goal of a WSN-CPS is active control and intervention in the physical environment.
They share three similarities: high data volume, stored data, and low latency processing.
And they differ because CPS places more emphasis on privacy and energy constraints, plus processing complexity.

scenes.title: Data management similarities
lines: The similarities in detail.
High data volume: both deal with large amounts of sensor data. Frequent sampling gives continuous, high volume streams that need efficient storage and processing.
Low latency processing: both must process data with minimal delay.
For example, a WSN monitoring tsunami activity must detect early warning signs quickly, while a WSN-CPS often has even stricter latency needs, for controlling actuators in real time.
Stored data: in both, collected data is stored for historical analysis, reporting, and decision making, revealing long term patterns and trends for decision support and prediction.

scenes.title: Data management differences
lines: The differences in detail.
Privacy: privacy is a higher priority in WSN-CPS, because it runs in sensitive areas like healthcare, autonomous vehicles and personal devices.
So privacy may dictate stricter data handling, storage, and transmission protocols.
Energy: both have energy limits, but they are more severe in WSN-CPS, because real time decision making and actuation need high intensity processing.
Energy efficient methods like data compression, aggregation, and intelligent routing are essential to prolong battery life.
Processing complexity: a WSN-CPS must transform raw data into actionable insights, extracting high level knowledge to make decisions.
A traditional WSN usually does only simple aggregation or statistical analysis, while WSN-CPS uses sophisticated algorithms, machine learning, and reasoning.

scenes.title: Constraints in WSN data management
lines: Constraints in WSN data management. There are four.
Energy consumption: sensors are battery powered and operate in remote locations, so designs must be energy efficient.
Memory and processing power: limited, due to small storage and computational capacity.
Data volume and real time processing: handling large, continuous data streams from sensors.
Data uncertainty: sensor data may be imprecise, due to environmental factors and technical limitations.

scenes.title: Comparing WSNs and CPS-WSNs
lines: Now the comparison table, on three criteria.
Mobility. In WSNs: limited controlled and uncontrolled mobility, mainly for network coverage.
In CPS-WSNs: controlled and uncontrolled mobility, typically mission oriented. Both sensing and actuating devices can be mobile.
Intelligence. In WSNs: data mining and knowledge discovery techniques detect high level events of interest, often using complex event processing.
In CPS-WSNs: there is a need to extract high level knowledge from heterogeneous sensing networks, and reasoning capabilities decide which actions to assign to the actuation component.
Real time constraint. In WSNs: important only for critical applications, such as tsunami monitoring.
In CPS-WSNs: more important, because the CPS must react in time and control the physical system. Delays are not commonly tolerated.

scenes.title: Key constraints in WSN-CPS
lines: So the key constraints in WSN-CPS data management are three.
Mobility: mobile devices improve network coverage, but increase network uncertainty.
Intelligence requirements: transforming raw data into actionable knowledge.
Real time constraints: ensuring timely response for applications that need immediate intervention.

scenes.title: Data management activities
lines: The data management activities.
Four key tasks for WSNs: data collection, data processing, data storage, and data querying.
CPS-WSNs add two more: data compression, and data analysis.
So six activities in total. We will go through each one.

scenes.title: Static and mobile WSN-CPS
lines: First, the types of WSN-CPS based on mobility.
A static WSN-CPS is built on stationary WSNs.
A mobile WSN-CPS incorporates mobile sensor nodes and systems.
Mobile WSN-CPS evolved from advances in robotics and embedded systems.
Mobile CPS, or MCPS, includes systems that can move and communicate across networks, like drones and mobile robots.

scenes.title: Data collection with mobile elements
lines: Activity one: data collection in mobile WSN-CPS.
Its purpose is to gather, acquire, or sample data efficiently, while conserving energy.
There are three types of mobile elements, or MEs.
Relocatable nodes move to improve network coverage and connectivity.
Mobile data collectors are mobile sinks or relays that gather data directly from sensor nodes.
Mobile peers are nodes that sense data and relay messages, forming a peer network.
Mobile data collection aims to balance sensing, communication, and processing, to minimize energy consumption.

scenes.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled mobility
lines: Controlled versus uncontrolled mobility.
With controlled mobility, mobile elements autonomously decide their paths based on goals, like maximizing data collection while minimizing energy use.
With uncontrolled mobility, paths are fixed or predictable, like public transportation, and movement is not managed by the system.
Controlled mobility can enhance data gathering in targeted areas.
Uncontrolled mobility applies when nodes cannot control their movements.

scenes.title: Data processing
lines: Activity two: data processing, which means applying transformations to raw sensor data.
Data cleaning removes errors and fills gaps in the data.
Data fusion combines data from multiple sources to enhance accuracy.
Different fusion types, sensor fusion, information fusion and data fusion, combine information for comprehensive analysis.

scenes.title: Data storage
lines: Activity three: data storage. The purpose is to store large data volumes efficiently, given limited memory, bandwidth, and energy.
Question one: what data to store? Real time applications may only keep recent data.
Question two: where to store it? There are three options.
Centralized storage: all data is sent to a base station. Good for centralized control, but it can create bottlenecks.
Distributed storage: data is stored closer to the sensors, reducing transmission costs and bottlenecks.
Hybrid approaches combine centralized and distributed storage, to balance efficiency.

scenes.title: Data querying
lines: Activity four: data querying, to retrieve relevant data based on specific requirements.
There are three querying models.
Abstract layer models provide a simplified view over the sensor data.
Statistical and model based techniques use probabilistic models for spatio temporal data.
Information Flow Processing, IFP, retrieves data from multiple sources in real time, and processes it for new insights.

scenes.title: Data compression
lines: Activity five, added in CPS: data compression.
The challenge: large data volumes need efficient storage and processing.
Compression techniques minimize storage size and conserve bandwidth.
Examples: stream compression, data aggregation, and reducing redundancy among data sources.

scenes.title: Data analysis
lines: Activity six: data analysis.
It analyzes sensor data to monitor and understand the real world environment.
A key task is atypical data detection: identifying unusual data patterns that may indicate significant events.
Examples of use: traffic congestion detection, and environmental monitoring.
The last slide lists the machine learning models used for such analysis: Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest, K Nearest Neighbours, and Support Vector Machine.

scenes.title: Exam recap
lines: Quick recap.
WSN-CPS integrates physical and cyber parts through wireless sensor networks, with four components: sensing, cyber, actuation, communication.
WSN goal is passive monitoring. WSN-CPS goal is active control. Same: volume, latency, storage. Different: privacy, energy, processing complexity.
Comparison criteria: mobility, intelligence, real time constraint.
Activities: collection, processing, storage, querying, plus compression and analysis in CPS.
Mobile elements: relocatable nodes, mobile data collectors, mobile peers. Storage: centralized, distributed, hybrid.
Good luck in your exam!
